summary: This document specifies using the Elliptic Curve Cryptography Brainpool curve groups for key exchange in IKEv2.

plainLanguage.summary: Brainpool curves are an alternative set of elliptic curves for cryptography. This RFC says how to use four of them for key exchange in IKEv2, the key exchange protocol. It also registers the four numbers that let two peers agree on which curve to use.

questions: how do i use brainpool in ikev2
which brainpool curve should i use
subtitle: How to negotiate one of the four Brainpool elliptic curves for key exchange in IKEv2.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 names the elliptic curve it will use for key exchange with a number from a registry, and no numbers had been assigned for the Brainpool curves.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers four Diffie-Hellman group transform IDs, 27 to 30, for brainpoolP224r1, brainpoolP256r1, brainpoolP384r1 and brainpoolP512r1, and fixes the encoding of the key exchange payload and the derivation of the shared secret for each of them.
tldr.outcome: An IKEv2 implementation can now offer the Brainpool curves for key exchange. The RFC also requires each peer to check that the coordinates it receives satisfy the curve equation, and warns that side-channel attacks need care when the twisted curves are used.

facts.label: Shared secret
facts.value: The x-coordinate of the Diffie-Hellman common value

today: RFC 6954 is an Informational RFC published in July 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated. Its practical effect is the four Diffie-Hellman group transform IDs it added to the IANA registry for IKEv2.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 5639 specified a new set of elliptic curve groups over finite prime fields for use in cryptographic applications. They are denoted as ECC Brainpool curves, they were generated in a verifiably pseudo-random way, and they comply with the security requirements of the relevant standards from ISO, ANSI, NIST and the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group.

The ASN.1 object identifiers defined in RFC 5639 already allow the Brainpool curves to be used in certificates and certificate revocation lists. Using them for key exchange in IKEv2 (RFC 5996) needs one more thing: IKEv2 names the curve it wants to use with a number from a registry of Diffie-Hellman group transform IDs, and no numbers had been assigned for the Brainpool curves. This document specifies transform IDs for four curves from RFC 5639, together with the encoding of the key exchange payload and the derivation of the shared secret when one of these curves is used.

The four curves covered are brainpoolP224r1, brainpoolP256r1, brainpoolP384r1 and brainpoolP512r1. The names carry the size of the curve: 224, 256, 384 and 512 bits. Appendix A of the RFC gives test vectors for a Diffie-Hellman exchange on each of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Brainpool curves are a standard set of elliptic curves for cryptography. IKEv2 needs a registered number for each curve it may use, and this RFC assigns four of those numbers for the Brainpool curves.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs
sections.content:
To use the ECC Brainpool curves for key exchange inside IKEv2, the Diffie-Hellman group transform IDs (Transform Type 4) listed below have been registered with IANA. The parameters associated with these curves are defined in RFC 5639.

  • brainpoolP224r1: transform ID 27
  • brainpoolP256r1: transform ID 28
  • brainpoolP384r1: transform ID 29
  • brainpoolP512r1: transform ID 30

Test vectors for the groups defined by the ECC Brainpool curves are provided in Appendix A of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each curve gets a number in the IKEv2 registry, from 27 to 30. The two peers exchange these numbers to agree on which curve to use.

sections.title: Using the Twisted Curves Internally
sections.content:
In RFC 5639, each random curve comes with a twisted curve, defined by a quadratic twist. The twisted curve offers the same level of security but potentially allows more efficient arithmetic, because the curve parameter A is -3. The transform IDs listed in the table also allow using the twisted curve that corresponds to the specified random curve.

Moving between the two curves is inexpensive. A point (x,y) on any of the listed curves can be transformed efficiently to the corresponding point (x',y') on the twisted curve of the same bit length, and back again, by setting (x',y') = (x*Z^2, y*Z^3) with the coefficient Z specified for that curve in RFC 5639.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Brainpool curve has a matching twisted version with the same security and simpler arithmetic. Points convert between the two with one formula, so an implementation can use whichever is faster.

sections.title: Key Exchange Payload and Shared Secret
sections.content:
The encoding of the key exchange payload and the derivation of the shared secret follow the methods specified in RFC 5903.

In an elliptic curve group over a prime field, which IKEv2 calls an ECP group, the Diffie-Hellman public value passed in a key establishment payload has two components, x and y, corresponding to the coordinates of an elliptic curve point. Each component MUST be computed from the corresponding coordinate using the FieldElement-to-OctetString conversion method specified in SEC 1, and each MUST have the bit length given in the table below. That method enforces the length, prepending the value with zeros if necessary.

The key exchange payload is the concatenation of the x and y coordinates, so it has twice the bit length of a single component. The Diffie-Hellman shared secret value consists only of the x value. It MUST be computed from the x-coordinate of the Diffie-Hellman common value using the same FieldElement-to-OctetString conversion method, and MUST have the bit length of a single component.
sections.plainLanguage: The public value sent to the peer holds two numbers, the x and y coordinates of a curve point. The shared secret uses only the x coordinate of the agreed point.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5996 apply accordingly. The RFC then adds the checks that matter for these curves.

To thwart certain active attacks, the validity of the other peer's public Diffie-Hellman value, recovered from the received key exchange payload, has to be verified. In particular, it MUST be verified that the x and y coordinates of the public value satisfy the curve equation. The RFC refers the reader to RFC 6989 for additional information.

The confidentiality, authenticity and integrity of a secure communication based on IKEv2 are limited by the weakest cryptographic primitive applied. To reach a maximum security level when using one of the elliptic curves in the table for key exchange, the RFC says to choose, following the recommendations of NIST Special Publication 800-57 and RFC 5639, the key derivation function, the algorithms and key lengths of symmetric encryption and message authentication, and the algorithm, bit length and hash function used for signature generation. The private Diffie-Hellman keys should be selected with the same bit length as the order of the group generated by the base point G and with approximately maximum entropy.

Implementations of elliptic curve cryptography for IKEv2 could be susceptible to side-channel attacks, where an attacker learns secrets from how the computation behaves. Particular care should be taken for implementations that internally use the corresponding twisted curve to take advantage of the efficient arithmetic that the special parameter A = -3 allows. The twisted curve offers the same level of security as the corresponding random curve through mathematical equivalence, but arithmetic based on small curve parameters could be harder to protect against side-channel attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peer must check that the coordinates it receives really lie on the curve, or an attacker could tamper with the exchange. The rest of the security depends on strong algorithms elsewhere, and on writing the arithmetic so that it does not leak secrets through timing.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has updated the Transform Type 4, Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs registry in the IKEv2 parameters registry to include the groups listed in Section 2.1, with transform IDs 27, 28, 29 and 30.
sections.plainLanguage: The four transform IDs are now in the IANA registry for IKEv2, so implementations can look them up by name.
